LESSON 4 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Assets, Threats, Vulnerabilities & Risk

Asset, threat, vulnerability, risk: four words in the right slots turn a vague worry into a specific fix you can make today.

Beginner3 min
Why this matters

Four words carry the whole of security: asset, threat, vulnerability, risk. Get them in the right slots and most arguments about security become much shorter.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • define each of the four words with an example of your own
  • take one system and fill all four slots for it
  • explain why a threat is not the same thing as a vulnerability

In plain English

Think about a bicycle you park on the street.

  • The bicycle is the asset: the thing you would hate to lose.
  • A thief is the threat: whatever could take it.
  • The cable lock that takes nine seconds to cut is the vulnerability.
  • The risk is how likely it is that those three meet — which depends on where you park, what the bike is worth, and how long you leave it.

Risk is not a fourth object in the list. It is the answer to "so what?" — the combination of how likely the loss is and how much it would hurt.

How it works

The reason the four words matter is that each one leads to a different fix, and people usually reach for the wrong one.

  • If the asset is not worth much, stop here. Removing the asset is a legitimate control and the cheapest one available.
  • If the threat can be avoided, avoid it. A service you do not run cannot be attacked.
  • If the vulnerability can be closed, close it — patching, a stronger lock, a fixed permission.
  • If none of those work, reduce the impact: insurance, backups, monitoring, and a plan for the day it happens.

Notice that "buy a firewall" is only one of those options, and not usually the first.

A worked example

A small online shop, described in the same four words:

  • Asset: the customer database, including email addresses and order history.
  • Threat: automated credential stuffing — bots replaying leaked email and password pairs from other breaches.
  • Vulnerability: the login page has no rate limit, and there is no second factor, so a leaked password is enough.
  • Risk: high, because the attack is automated, cheap, and does not need to know anything about this particular shop.

The fix follows from the vulnerability, not from the threat. You cannot stop bots existing. You can rate-limit logins and require a second factor, which turns a cheap automated attack into an expensive manual one.

The mistake most beginners make

Confusing a threat with a vulnerability. "Hackers" is a threat; "our admin panel has no password" is a vulnerability. You cannot fix the first, and you can fix the second today.

The other mistake is treating risk as a yes-or-no. Every system has some risk. The question is whether the risk is understood, accepted and priced — not whether it exists.

Try it in two minutes

Choose one system you use — a phone, a folder, a website — and write four lines:

  • Asset: what specifically would I lose?
  • Threat: who or what could cause that?
  • Vulnerability: what specific gap lets them succeed?
  • Risk: how likely is it, and how much would it cost me?

If you cannot name a specific vulnerability, you have not found it yet — and that is the line to go and look at properly.

Practice / apply

Pick one system you actually use — a phone, a website, a shared folder — and fill in the four words on paper.

Key takeaways

  • Asset, threat, vulnerability — three different things, three different fixes.
  • Risk is likelihood times impact, not a yes-or-no question.
  • You cannot remove a threat, but you can usually close a vulnerability.
  • Removing or not holding the asset is a real control, and often the cheapest.
